title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: mixedsubjects package provides tools analyzing randomized experiments combine traditional human subjects data predictions large language models (LLMs) machine learning algorithms. approach, call Mixed-Subjects Design (MSD), can substantially increase precision treatment effect estimates maintaining valid statistical inference.

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Running experiments human subjects expensive. typical survey response might cost several dollars, detecting small treatment effects often requires thousands participants. Meanwhile, LLMs can generate predictions humans might respond experimental treatments fraction cost—often less cent per prediction. key insight behind mixed-subjects designs LLM predictions, even imperfect, contain information human behavior. combining smaller sample actual human responses (“gold standard”) larger pool LLM predictions, can: Reduce variance treatment effect estimates Maintain valid inference—confidence intervals correct coverage Lower costs experimentation Importantly, approach assume LLM predictions accurate. Even predictions biased, methods package automatically adjust bias using human subjects data.

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: mixedsubjects package implements seven estimators Average Treatment Effect (ATE) mixed-subjects designs: package also helps design optimal experiments determining allocate budget human subjects LLM predictions.

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Imagine ’re running survey experiment test whether persuasive message changes attitudes. : 200 human respondents completed survey (100 treated, 100 control) 1,000 LLM predictions additional respondents answered
code: set.seed(123)  # True treatment effect true_ate <- 0.3  # Human subjects data (observed) n_observed <- 200 observed_df <- data.frame(   # Treatment assignment (balanced)   D = rep(c(1, 0), each = n_observed / 2) )  # Generate outcomes: Y(0) ~ N(0, 1), Y(1) ~ N(0.3, 1) observed_df$Y <- ifelse(   observed_df$D == 1,   rnorm(n_observed / 2, mean = true_ate, sd = 1),   rnorm(n_observed / 2, mean = 0, sd = 1) )  # LLM predictions (correlated with true outcomes, but with some error) # S^(1) predicts Y(1), S^(0) predicts Y(0) observed_df$S1 <- 0.6 * observed_df$Y + rnorm(n_observed, 0, 0.5) observed_df$S0 <- 0.5 * observed_df$Y + rnorm(n_observed, 0, 0.6)  # Unobserved units (only have predictions, no actual Y) # Predictions must come from the same pipeline as observed (Assumption C: Random Labeling) n_unobserved <- 1000 D_unobs <- rep(c(1, 0), each = n_unobserved / 2) latent_Y <- ifelse(D_unobs == 1,                    rnorm(n_unobserved / 2, mean = true_ate, sd = 1),                    rnorm(n_unobserved / 2, mean = 0, sd = 1)) unobserved_df <- data.frame(   D = D_unobs,   S1 = 0.6 * latent_Y + rnorm(n_unobserved, 0, 0.5),   S0 = 0.5 * latent_Y + rnorm(n_unobserved, 0, 0.6) )

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package

code: msd <- msd_data(observed = observed_df, unobserved = unobserved_df) print(msd) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Data #> ========================== #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed (labeled):     200  #>     - Treated (D=1):      100  #>     - Control (D=0):      100  #>   Unobserved (unlabeled): 1000  #>  #> Predictions Available: #>   S0 (control arm):   Yes  #>   S1 (treatment arm): Yes  #>  #> Column Mapping (original names): #>   Observed:  Y=Y, D=D, S0=S0, S1=S1 #>   Unobserved: D=D, S0=S0, S1=S1 #>  #> Available Estimators: #>   - DiM:     Yes (no predictions needed) #>   - GREG:    Yes #>   - PPI++:   Yes #>   - D-T:     Yes #>   - DiP:     Yes (both S0 and S1 available) #>   - DiP++:   Yes #>   - D-T DiP: Yes

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: mixed-subjects design, need: Y: outcome variable D: Treatment indicator (1 = treated, 0 = control) S1 /S0: LLM predictions (optional DiM) D: Treatment indicator S1 /S0: LLM predictions

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: package distinguishes two prediction setups: Setup 1: Arm-specific predictions (1 prediction per unit) unit prediction assigned treatment condition: - Treated units S(1)S^{(1)} (prediction outcome treatment) - Control units S(0)S^{(0)} (prediction outcome control) typical ask LLM predict unit’s response actual assigned condition. Setup 2: predictions (2 predictions per unit) unit predictions conditions: - S(1)S^{(1)}: Prediction outcome treated - S(0)S^{(0)}: Prediction outcome control requires asking LLM predict unit’s response conditions, doubles prediction cost enables DiP family estimators.

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: msd_data() function accepts data two formats: Option 1: Separate dataframes Option 2: Combined dataframe data single dataframe unobserved units Y = NA:
code: msd <- msd_data(   observed = observed_df,    # Must have Y, D, and optionally S0, S1   unobserved = unobserved_df # Must have D and S0, S1 (no Y) ) # Combine into single dataframe combined_df <- rbind(   observed_df,   data.frame(Y = NA, D = unobserved_df$D,              S0 = unobserved_df$S0, S1 = unobserved_df$S1) )  # Create msd_data object msd_combined <- msd_data(data = combined_df) print(msd_combined) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Data #> ========================== #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed (labeled):     200  #>     - Treated (D=1):      100  #>     - Control (D=0):      100  #>   Unobserved (unlabeled): 1000  #>  #> Predictions Available: #>   S0 (control arm):   Yes  #>   S1 (treatment arm): Yes  #>  #> Column Mapping (original names): #>   Observed:  Y=Y, D=D, S0=S0, S1=S1 #>   Unobserved: D=D, S0=S0, S1=S1 #>  #> Available Estimators: #>   - DiM:     Yes (no predictions needed) #>   - GREG:    Yes #>   - PPI++:   Yes #>   - D-T:     Yes #>   - DiP:     Yes (both S0 and S1 available) #>   - DiP++:   Yes #>   - D-T DiP: Yes

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: default, package expects columns named Y (outcome), D (treatment), S0 (control prediction), S1 (treatment prediction). columns use different names, specify explicitly: can even use different column names observed unobserved data:
code: # Custom column names my_data <- data.frame(   response_var = rnorm(100),   is_treated = rep(c(1, 0), each = 50),   claude_pred_ctrl = rnorm(100),   claude_pred_trt = rnorm(100) )  msd <- msd_data(   observed = my_data,   outcome = "response_var",   treatment = "is_treated",   pred_control = "claude_pred_ctrl",   pred_treated = "claude_pred_trt" ) msd <- msd_data(   observed = obs_df,   unobserved = unobs_df,   obs_outcome = "Y",   obs_treatment = "treated",   obs_pred_control = "gpt_pred_0",   obs_pred_treated = "gpt_pred_1",   unobs_treatment = "D",   unobs_pred_control = "S0",   unobs_pred_treated = "S1" )

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: even flexibility, can use formula interface directly estimator functions. similar syntax used ivreg regression packages: formula three parts: 1. Left ~: outcome variable name 2. ~ |: treatment indicator variable name 3. |: prediction variable name(s) DiM (doesn’t use predictions), can omit prediction part:
code: # Formula: outcome ~ treatment | predictions # Using custom column names directly in the estimator  # For GREG-type estimators (single prediction per arm) result <- msd_greg(response ~ treatment | pred_1 + pred_0,                    observed = obs_df, unobserved = unobs_df)  # For DiP-type estimators (both predictions) result <- msd_dt_dip(Y ~ D | S1 + S0,                      observed = obs_df, unobserved = unobs_df) result <- msd_dim(response ~ treated, observed = obs_df)

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: classical estimator ignores LLM predictions entirely: τ̂DiM=Y‾1−Y‾0\hat{\tau}^{DiM} = \bar{Y}_1 - \bar{Y}_0 Use baseline. ’s unbiased requires predictions.
code: result <- msd_dim(msd) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: Difference-in-Means (DiM)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.4980  #> Standard Error:  0.1330  #> 95% CI:         [0.2373, 0.7586] #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: GREG uses predictions “calibrate” estimate: τ̂GREG=[S‾U(1)+(Y‾1−S‾O1(1))]−[S‾U(0)+(Y‾0−S‾O0(0))]\hat{\tau}^{GREG} = \left[\bar{S}^{(1)}_U + (\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{S}^{(1)}_{O_1})\right] - \left[\bar{S}^{(0)}_U + (\bar{Y}_0 - \bar{S}^{(0)}_{O_0})\right] adjusts prediction mean observed “rectifier” (average prediction error labeled data).
code: result <- msd_greg(msd) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: GREG (lambda = 1)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.3307  #> Standard Error:  0.1073  #> 95% CI:         [0.1203, 0.5410] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda:        1.0000  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: PPI++ improves GREG estimating optimal tuning parameter λ\lambda: μ̂dPPI(λ)=Y‾d+λ(S‾U(d)−S‾O(d))\hat{\mu}_d^{PPI}(\lambda) = \bar{Y}_d + \lambda(\bar{S}^{(d)}_U - \bar{S}^{(d)}_O) λ=1\lambda = 1, equals GREG. PPI++ estimates λ\lambda minimize variance using cross-fitting.
code: result <- msd_ppi(msd, n_folds = 2) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: PPI++ (cross-fit, K=2)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.3617  #> Standard Error:  0.1033  #> 95% CI:         [0.1593, 0.5642] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda:        0.8222  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: D-T uses separate tuning parameters arm (λ1\lambda_1 treatment, λ0\lambda_0 control): τ̂D−T=μ̂1PPI(λ1)−μ̂0PPI(λ0)\hat{\tau}^{D-T} = \hat{\mu}_1^{PPI}(\lambda_1) - \hat{\mu}_0^{PPI}(\lambda_0) useful prediction quality differs treatment control conditions.
code: result <- msd_dt(msd, n_folds = 2) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: D-T (Doubly-Tuned, cross-fit, K=2)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.3457  #> Standard Error:  0.1037  #> 95% CI:         [0.1425, 0.5489] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda_1 (treatment):  0.9039  #>   lambda_0 (control):    0.7806  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: DiP uses contrast S(1)−S(0)S^{(1)} - S^{(0)} unlabeled unit: τ̂DiP=S(1)−S(0)¯U+(Y‾1−S‾O1(1))−(Y‾0−S‾O0(0))\hat{\tau}^{DiP} = \overline{S^{(1)} - S^{(0)}}_U + (\bar{Y}_1 - \bar{S}^{(1)}_{O_1}) - (\bar{Y}_0 - \bar{S}^{(0)}_{O_0}) Key insight: S(1)S^{(1)} S(0)S^{(0)} positively correlated (often —units score high treatment also tend score high control), variance difference smaller sum individual variances.
code: result <- msd_dip(msd) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: DiP (Difference-in-Predictions, lambda = 1)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.1454  #> Standard Error:  0.0976  #> 95% CI:         [-0.0459, 0.3367] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda:        1.0000  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: DiP++ applies power-tuning DiP estimator single λ\lambda: τ̂DiP++(λ)=λ⋅S(1)−S(0)¯U+(Y‾1−λS‾O1(1))−(Y‾0−λS‾O0(0))\hat{\tau}^{DiP++}(\lambda) = \lambda \cdot \overline{S^{(1)} - S^{(0)}}_U + (\bar{Y}_1 - \lambda\bar{S}^{(1)}_{O_1}) - (\bar{Y}_0 - \lambda\bar{S}^{(0)}_{O_0})
code: result <- msd_dip_pp(msd, n_folds = 2) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: DiP++ (cross-fit, K=2)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.1891  #> Standard Error:  0.0965  #> 95% CI:         [0.0000, 0.3782] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda:        0.8804  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: flexible estimator combines DiP arm-specific tuning: τ̂D−TDiP=λ1S(1)−λ0S(0)¯U+(Y‾1−λ1S‾O1(1))−(Y‾0−λ0S‾O0(0))\hat{\tau}^{D-T\ DiP} = \overline{\lambda_1 S^{(1)} - \lambda_0 S^{(0)}}_U + (\bar{Y}_1 - \lambda_1\bar{S}^{(1)}_{O_1}) - (\bar{Y}_0 - \lambda_0\bar{S}^{(0)}_{O_0})
code: result <- msd_dt_dip(msd, n_folds = 2) print(result) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design Estimation #> ================================= #> Estimator: D-T DiP (cross-fit, K=2)  #>  #> Point Estimate:  0.1571  #> Standard Error:  0.0966  #> 95% CI:         [-0.0323, 0.3465] #>  #> Tuning Parameters: #>   lambda_1 (treatment):  0.9944  #>   lambda_0 (control):    0.8544  #>  #> Sample Sizes: #>   Observed:   n_1=100, n_0=100 #>   Unobserved: |U|=1000

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Use estimate_all() run applicable estimators :
code: all_results <- estimate_all(msd) print(all_results) #>  #> Mixed-Subjects Design: All Estimators #> ====================================== #>  #>                                    Estimator Estimate     SE 95% CI Lower #>                    Difference-in-Means (DiM)   0.4980 0.1330       0.2373 #>                            GREG (lambda = 1)   0.3307 0.1073       0.1203 #>                       PPI++ (cross-fit, K=2)   0.3664 0.1032       0.1643 #>           D-T (Doubly-Tuned, cross-fit, K=2)   0.3585 0.1034       0.1557 #>  DiP (Difference-in-Predictions, lambda = 1)   0.1454 0.0976      -0.0459 #>                       DiP++ (cross-fit, K=2)   0.1893 0.0965       0.0002 #>                     D-T DiP (cross-fit, K=2)   0.1772 0.0966      -0.0121 #>  95% CI Upper #>        0.7586 #>        0.5410 #>        0.5686 #>        0.5612 #>        0.3367 #>        0.3785 #>        0.3665

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: ’s practical guide choosing estimator:
code: Do you have LLM predictions? ├── No → Use DiM └── Yes → Do you have BOTH S^(1) and S^(0) for each unit?     ├── No (only arm-specific) →     │   └── Is prediction quality similar across arms?     │       ├── Yes → Use PPI++     │       └── No → Use D-T     └── Yes (both predictions) →         └── Are S^(1) and S^(0) positively correlated?             ├── Yes → Use D-T DiP (recommended)             └── No/Unsure → Use D-T

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: optimal_design() function finds allocation minimizes expected variance given budget constraints:
code: design <- optimal_design(   pilot_data = msd,          # Pilot study data   budget = 5000,             # Total budget in dollars   cost_human = 5,            # $5 per human response   cost_prediction = 0.01,    # $0.01 per LLM prediction   treatment_prob = 0.5       # Balanced treatment assignment )  print(design) #>  #> Optimal Mixed-Subjects Design #> ============================== #>  #> Recommended Design: #>   Estimator:         DT_DIP  #>   Observed units:    970  #>     - Treated:       485  #>     - Control:       485  #>   Unobserved units:  7500  #>  #> Expected Performance: #>   Variance:  0.0019  #>   SE:        0.0431  #>  #> Budget: #>   Total:    $5,000 #>   Used:     $5,000 #>   Human:    $5/observation #>   Predict:  $0.01/prediction #>  #> Comparison Across Estimators: #>  Estimator n_obs n_unobs     SE #>        DIM  1000       0 0.0595 #>       GREG   951   24500 0.0443 #>        PPI   960   20000 0.0439 #>         DT   960   20000 0.0438 #>        DIP   960   10000 0.0438 #>     DIP_PP   970    7500 0.0434 #>     DT_DIP   970    7500 0.0431

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: ’s recommended workflow using mixed-subjects designs research:

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Run small pilot study human subjects LLM predictions:
code: # Collect pilot data pilot_observed <- collect_human_responses(n = 100) pilot_observed$S1 <- get_llm_predictions(pilot_observed, condition = "treatment") pilot_observed$S0 <- get_llm_predictions(pilot_observed, condition = "control")  pilot_unobserved <- generate_synthetic_units(n = 200) pilot_unobserved$S1 <- get_llm_predictions(pilot_unobserved, condition = "treatment") pilot_unobserved$S0 <- get_llm_predictions(pilot_unobserved, condition = "control")  pilot_msd <- msd_data(observed = pilot_observed, unobserved = pilot_unobserved)

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Examine well LLM predictions correlate actual outcomes:
code: # Check correlations pilot_results <- estimate_all(pilot_msd) print(pilot_results)  # Compare to DiM baseline dim_se <- pilot_results$SE[pilot_results$Estimator == "Difference-in-Means (DiM)"] best_se <- min(pilot_results$SE) variance_reduction <- 1 - (best_se / dim_se)^2 cat("Potential variance reduction:", round(variance_reduction * 100, 1), "%\n")

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Use pilot data design main study:
code: design <- optimal_design(   pilot_data = pilot_msd,   budget = 10000,   cost_human = 5,   cost_prediction = 0.01 ) print(design)

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Collect data according design:
code: # Collect human responses main_observed <- collect_human_responses(n = design$optimal_n_obs)  # Generate LLM predictions main_observed$S1 <- get_llm_predictions(main_observed, "treatment") main_observed$S0 <- get_llm_predictions(main_observed, "control")  main_unobserved <- generate_synthetic_units(n = design$optimal_n_unobs) main_unobserved$S1 <- get_llm_predictions(main_unobserved, "treatment") main_unobserved$S0 <- get_llm_predictions(main_unobserved, "control")  main_msd <- msd_data(observed = main_observed, unobserved = main_unobserved)

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: Estimate treatment effect using recommended estimator:
code: # Run the recommended estimator result <- msd_dt_dip(main_msd)  # Or whichever was recommended print(result)  # Optionally verify with bootstrap boot_result <- bootstrap_variance(main_msd, "dt_dip", n_bootstrap = 1000)

what: Q: What if my LLM predictions are biased?
title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: : ’s fine! MSD estimators designed valid even predictions biased. human subjects data used “rectify” systematic bias predictions. still get unbiased estimates valid confidence intervals.

what: Q: How much do predictions need to correlate with outcomes?
title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: : positive correlation helps, better. rough guide: - ρ>0.3\rho > 0.3: Modest variance reduction - ρ>0.5\rho > 0.5: Substantial variance reduction - ρ>0.7\rho > 0.7: Large variance reduction can estimate correlation pilot data.

what: Q: Can I use predictions from multiple LLMs?

text: : current package supports one set predictions. multiple LLMs, : 1. Use single best-performing LLM 2. Average predictions across LLMs using 3. Use LLM whose predictions highest correlation outcomes

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: MSD estimators require: Random sampling: observed unobserved units drawn population Random treatment assignment: Treatment randomly assigned pools Independent predictions: LLM predictions don’t use observed outcomes Finite variances: Standard regularity conditions

title: Introduction to Mixed-Subjects Designs with the mixedsubjects Package
text: reference, variance formulas key estimators: DiM: Var(τ̂DiM)=σY(1)2n1+σY(0)2n0Var(\hat{\tau}^{DiM}) = \frac{\sigma^2_{Y(1)}}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma^2_{Y(0)}}{n_0} GREG: Var(τ̂GREG)=∑d∈{0,1}[σS(d)2md+Var(Y(d)−S(d))nd]Var(\hat{\tau}^{GREG}) = \sum_{d \\{0,1\}} \left[\frac{\sigma^2_{S^{(d)}}}{m_d} + \frac{Var(Y(d) - S^{(d)})}{n_d}\right] DiP: Var(τ̂DiP)=Var(S(1)−S(0))m+∑d∈{0,1}Var(Y(d)−S(d))ndVar(\hat{\tau}^{DiP}) = \frac{Var(S^{(1)} - S^{(0)})}{m} + \sum_{d \\{0,1\}} \frac{Var(Y(d) - S^{(d)})}{n_d} tuned estimators (PPI++, D-T, DiP++, D-T DiP) complex variance formulas account estimation tuning parameters.
